cover.title: Insertion sort
cover.lead: Sort like a hand of cards: each new card slides left past every bigger card.
cover.use_it_when: The input is small, or almost sorted: insertion sort does very little work there.
cover.why_it_matters: It's the first of three basic sorts. Selection and bubble sort come next.

slides.title: A hand of cards
slides.scene: You pick up cards one at a time. Each new card slides left past every bigger card.

blocks.text: The cards in your hand stay sorted. That hand is the [[sorted part]], and it grows by one card each time.

slides.title: Watch the gap
slides.lead: Pass 3 of the video, up close. The gap walks left until the card fits.

quickcheck.question: Insertion sort on 4 3 2 1. How many shifts in total?
quickcheck.answer: Answer: {{shifts([4, 3, 2, 1])}} shifts. The 3 makes 1, the 2 makes 2, the 1 makes 3.

slides.label: WHEN IT'S FAST
slides.teaser: The answer, and when it's fast
slides.title: Fast when almost sorted

blocks.text: Each shift fixes one pair that is out of order. So the work grows with how unsorted the input is.

slides.title: Insertion sort
slides.explain: Line 5 checks the value on the left. Lines 6 and 7 shift it right; line 8 drops the card in.

slides.title: Save the card first
slides.lead: Skip line 3 and use nums[i] in lines 5 and 8. Line 6 writes over nums[i], so the card is lost.

wrong.note: The first shift copies 5 over the 2.

cost.note: Reversed input needs n(n − 1)/2 shifts. Sorted input needs only n − 1 compares.
